newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief promises to usher in a time for healing.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief promises to usher in a time for healing.

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Thursday promised wide-ranging changes in the United Nations but said reforms could not be instituted with arbitrary cuts in staff or vital programmes.

In his first speech to U.N. employees, he promised to usher in a time for healing -- of the financial crisis, of a "crisis of faith" between the world body and member states and of morale among the staff.
As the first secretary-general to be chosen from the ranks of career U.N. officials, Annan was greeted with a standing ovation by the staff as one of their own.
"I do not believe the disjointed incrementalism of the past with its baggage of duplications and overlaps was a positive evolution," he said.
"Equally, I have never believed that disjointed downsizing, with arbitrary staff cuts that weaken essential capabilities, can bring real improvement," he said.

"It is not reform when, for lack of funds we have to turn our backs on massacres and suffering and collapse of civil society," he said. "Real reform will enable us to put in place new mechanisms for confronting the world's political and economic crises promptly, courageoulsy and efficiently."

Annan said some units, functions and occupations would probably be cut. But he said governments would no longer be allowed to vote limits on salaries of U.N. staff while at the same time subsidising wages for their own nationals.

As secretary-general Annan is mainly in charge of an estimated 9,000 employees in the secretariat in New York, Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi, whose numbers have been cut 10 percent cut over the last two years and 20 percent in the last 10 years. But tens of thousands of other employees, not all of them under his control, belong to separate agencies and commissions.
Since he took office on Jan. 1, the 58-year old Ghanaian has promised to come up with a plan to streamline the entire structure and ask member states to approve it.

But his approach differs from that of Washington and especially conservatives in Congress, who speak of reform primarily in terms of drastic staff cuts. The United States owes $1.3 billion in dues and peacekeeping expenses, more than half of arrears due to the world body.
The Clinton administration blocked a second five-year term for Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, primarily because of allegations he did not move quickly enough on reform.
Referring to the criticism of the world body, Annan said the "next five years must be, above, all a time for healing."
"We must heal the financial crisis of the organisation, which cannot be expected to move forward if it is dragged down by the burden of unpaid dues," he said.
"But at the bottom the financial crisis is a political crisis -- a crisis of faith in the organisation.
"It is up to us to prove to the member states that their contributions are used wisely and efficiently for the implementation of programmes which they have mandated."
Referring to criticism of U.N. staff, he said he was aware that much of it was arbitrary and unfair.
"But the burden of proof is on us. The excellence of our performance will turn our detractors into supporters," he said, adding: We all know nobody argues with success."
He pledged a new "management culture" that would hold senior officials accountable for performance of their staff.

Annan said he once read that "the worst thing that can happen to you in your career is to get to the top of the ladder only to find that it's been placed against the wrong wall." But he said service with the United Nations was not a job but a "calling" and that no one joined to get famous or to live a life of comfort.
